estimates.narrative: Across multiple official and expert sources, the UK is moving toward a default 10-year ILR waiting period under an earned settlement model, with changes expected around 2026. While exemptions and transitional rules exist, the consensus indicates a 10-year baseline for most migrants by May 2026, yielding a calibrated posterior near 0.97.
summary: Official materials indicate the baseline settlement waiting period will move to 10 years under an earned settlement framework with carve-outs.
Implementation is targeted for 2026, making the 10-year baseline highly likely for most migrants before May 2026.
Although there are route-specific exemptions (high-skill, public service) and transitional arrangements, the overall direction supports a near-term shift to 10 years.
Parliamentary momentum and multiple forecasters support the policy trajectory.

question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: Official materials explicitly describe a default 10-year ILR waiting period under an earned settlement framework, with reductions based on contributions and other criteria.
Implementation is targeted for 2026 (around April–May), suggesting the 10-year baseline will apply to many migrants before May 2026, though not universally due to route-specific carve-outs.
The long-residence route already uses a 10-year benchmark, reinforcing feasibility of a broader shift to 10 years for settlement.
Adversarial objections highlight real risks of delays and transitional rules that could slow universal adoption; the direction remains strongly toward a 10-year baseline but with exceptions.

justification.critique_assessment: The objections identify plausible implementation risks (delays, transitional arrangements, route-specific carve-outs) that could temper universal adoption by May 2026, revealing a genuine but not fatal blind spot in assuming universal, immediate effect.
justification.adjustment: Adjusted downward from the ensemble 0.93 to 0.90 to reflect near-term risks of delay and non-uniform application, while acknowledging the strong policy trajectory toward a 10-year baseline by 2026.

forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration policy reforms implementing a 'earned settlement' model that raises the baseline ILR qualifying period to 10 years (with exceptions) and ties settlement to contributions and other criteria

sources.claim: The starting point for settlement will move from 5 years to 10 years, introducing an earned settlement concept with a four-pillar framework.
The government outlines an earned settlement model with a default 10-year qualifying period, subject to reductions based on contributions across four pillars.

The House of Commons Library summarizes the November 2025 announcement that the baseline qualifying period would be 10 years for many migrants, with various carve-outs (e.g., higher-skilled workers may still qualify earlier).
Migration Observatory notes the standard waiting period increasing from five to ten years, with important exceptions and differentiated timelines by skill level and route.
GOV.UK confirms the Long Residence route requires 10 years of lawful residence toward settlement.
The consultation material reiterates the 10-year default and establishes a framework for time-adjusted improvements based on character, integration, contribution, and residence.

House of Commons Library notes that the May 2025 immigration white paper proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for permanent residence from five to ten years, with some groups able to qualify sooner; changes expected to begin around April 2026.

GOV.UK consultation states the default qualifying period for settlement will be increased to ten years, with potential reductions based on contributions, under an earned settlement model (Updated November 2025).
Current long-residence guidance confirms a 10-year qualifying period for settlement under the long-residence route, illustrating the 10-year benchmark within immigration policy.
The Earned Settlement consultation states the default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from five to ten years, with exceptions.
House of Commons Library briefing confirms government plans to raise the baseline waiting period to ten years, announced 20 November 2025.
Migration Observatory summarizes the changes as a ten-year baseline with exceptions depending on circumstances.
The Guardian reports the government proposed to extend the waiting period to ten years for permanent settlement.
Moore SGD Law notes the consultation closes February 12, 2026, with potential changes taking effect as early as April 2026.

synthesis: Evidence points to a 10-year default for settlement being implemented around 2026 for most migrants, with carve-outs and transitional arrangements creating non-uniform effects. The likelihood is high, but there is non-negligible risk of delays or partial adoption that keeps the outcome uncertain in the very near term.
